description.text: Psiche (Ψυχή) is a figure of Greek mythology who personifies the concept of the soul (psyché), encompassing the soul’s emotional movements and, by extension, the idea of a soulmate or human love. Her story begins with a youthful beauty that incites the jealousy of Aphrodite, who orders Cupid (Eros) to make Psiche fall for a base man. Instead, Cupid falls in love with her and visits her nightly in a magnificent palace, revealing himself only in darkness and instructing her never to look upon his face.

When Psiche’s curiosity leads her to light a lamp over Cupid’s sleeping form, a drop of hot oil falls on him, awakening him and causing him to abandon her. She then embarks on a series of arduous trials set by Aphrodite—sorting grain, gathering golden fleece, and retrieving a fragment of beauty from the underworld—before ultimately returning to Olympus. There, after a divine intervention that heals her sleep, she marries Eros, is granted immortality, and is transformed into a goddess who protects young girls. The couple’s daughter, named Edone (or Voluptas in Roman tradition), embodies the notion of pleasure.

curiosities.text: The tale of Eros and Psiche, especially as recounted in Apuleius’s *Metamorphoses*, captivated Renaissance artists, who depicted its episodes in the decorative schemes of noble palaces.
Psiche’s name is the root of the modern English word “psyche,” meaning soul, reflecting her symbolic role as the embodiment of the human spirit.
Her daughter Edone, also called Voluptas in Roman mythology, literally means “pleasure,” underscoring the thematic link between love, beauty, and joy in the myth.
